extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers, and policymakers interested in multilateral development banks and international development (Asian Development Bank)
extracted.subtask_short: adb institutional policy and operations overview
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article giving an overview of the Asian Development Bank's mission, governance, financing instruments, operational focus areas, policies (including access to information and safeguards), notable projects, and criticisms. Useful for understanding how ADB operates and the standards it reports and is evaluated against.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim / mission
rubrics_metrics.description: The ADB defines itself as a social development organization that is dedicated to reducing poverty in Asia and the Pacific through inclusive economic growth, environmentally sustainable growth, and regional integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carried out through investments (loans, grants and information sharing) in infrastructure, health care services, financial and public administration systems, climate change preparedness, natural resource management, and other areas; scholars (ADB-JSP) expected to contribute to economic and social development of their home countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core operational focus — Education
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is named as a core operational area; most developing countries in Asia and the Pacific have seen dramatic rises in primary enrollment but face remaining challenges threatening economic and social growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ADB programs target education gaps as part of poverty reduction and inclusive growth efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core operational focus — Environment, climate change, and disaster risk management
rubrics_metrics.description: Environmental sustainability is considered a prerequisite for economic growth and poverty reduction in Asia and the Pacific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ADB invests in climate initiatives, disaster response and risk management, and projects that help countries prepare for the impact of climate change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core operational focus — Finance sector development
rubrics_metrics.description: The financial system is described as the lifeline of a country's economy; ADB prioritizes financial sector and capital market development, including microfinance, SMEs, and regulatory reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PSOD and other departments support trade finance, microfinance, and reforms to expand inclusive access to finance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core operational focus — Infrastructure (transport, communications, energy, water, urban development)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infrastructure (transport and communications, energy, water supply and sanitation, and urban development) is one of the principal operational areas for ADB lending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ADB finances large-scale infrastructure projects to support economic growth and regional connectivity (examples in country project lists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Core operational focus — Regional cooperation and integration (RCI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional cooperation and integration is an operational priority intended to make national economies more regionally connected to accelerate growth, reduce poverty, raise productivity and employment, and strengthen institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RCI initiatives support trade, cross-border infrastructure and coordinated policies across member countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core operational focus — Private sector lending (PSOD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Private Sector Lending became a priority and the Private Sector Operations Department finances non-sovereign operations (debt, equity, mezzanine finance) for projects with social benefits; the Bank set a target that PSOD should constitute 50% of the bank's lending by 2020 (per the Long Term Strategic Framework adopted in 2008).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PSOD grew rapidly from 2002; it provides broader instruments (guarantees, equity, mezzanine) and aims to leverage commercial finance while achieving social development outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financing types and eligibility (hard vs soft loans)
rubrics_metrics.description: ADB offers 'hard' loans on commercial terms primarily to middle-income countries and 'soft' loans with lower interest rates to poorer countries; based on a policy change both types were to be sourced from the ordinary capital resources (OCR) starting January 2017.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of instrument depends on country income/eligibility; PSOD can also structure non-sovereign financings including guarantees, equity and mezzanine finance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private sector participation limits and social-return requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: ADB provides direct financial assistance to private sector companies for projects that have clear social benefits beyond the financial rate of return; ADB's participation is usually limited and it normally holds no more than 25% of any given transaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ADB's role is to leverage commercial funding and crowd-in private capital rather than to be majority financier; emphasis on projects that generate social as well as financial returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-financing practice
rubrics_metrics.description: ADB partners with other development organizations and co-financiers on some projects to increase the amount of funding available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 2014 nearly half of ADB's $22.9 billion in operations were financed by other organizations; co-financing is a standard practice to scale impact and share risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to information policy (presumed disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: ADB has an information disclosure policy that presumes all information produced by the institution should be disclosed to the public unless there is a specific reason to keep it confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy calls for accountability and timely responses to requests for information; explicit exceptions include information that jeopardizes personal privacy, safety and security, certain financial and commercial information, and other specified exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance structure — Board of Governors / Board of Directors / President
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest policy-making body is the Board of Governors (one representative per member state); the Board of Governors elects twelve members of the Board of Directors and their deputies, and elects the bank's president who chairs the Board of Directors and manages ADB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: President serves a five-year term and may be re-elected; historically the president has been Japanese due to shareholder patterns; governance distinguishes regional vs non-regional members (eight of twelve directors from regional members).

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting system — weighted voting by capital subscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: ADB uses a weighted voting system in which votes are distributed in proportion to members' capital subscriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major shareholders (e.g., Japan and the United States) hold the largest proportions of shares and therefore greater voting power; the institution issues an annual report summarizing operations and budget for public review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental and social safeguard policies (indigenous peoples, involuntary resettlement, environment)
rubrics_metrics.description: ADB maintains environmental safeguards and policies for indigenous peoples and involuntary resettlement that are intended to meet international standards on paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics allege these safeguards are often ignored in practice, are too vague or weak to be effective, or are not enforced, leading to social and environmental damage in some large-scale projects (e.g., Mae Moh coal-fired power station).

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership eligibility and classification (regional vs non-regional; graduation)
rubrics_metrics.description: ADB admits members of the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP) and non-regional developed countries; it distinguishes between regional members (Asia-Pacific) and non-regional members, with regional members being main beneficiaries and non-regional members primarily contributing capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members are classified for financing eligibility (ADF/OCR groups) and there is a graduation policy for developing member countries; membership details include accession dates and capital share arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding sources and financial positioning (bond issuance, member contributions, retained earnings)
rubrics_metrics.description: ADB obtains funding by issuing bonds on the world's capital markets, contributions of member countries, retained earnings from lending operations, and repayment of loans; Moody's assigned a AAA rating to its senior unsecured debt (as of April 2025).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ADB also issues local-currency instruments (e.g., rupee-linked bonds) to support development of local capital markets and raise funds in different currencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic financing targets and institutional reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: ADB has set strategic targets in documents such as the Long Term Strategic Framework (LTSF), including a target that assistance to private sector development should constitute 50% of the bank's lending by 2020 and increasing annual lending and grants (e.g., OCR expansion to permit $20 billion annual lending by 2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional reforms and resource mobilization (capital increases, ADF-OCR merger) are used to meet these strategic targets; performance against such targets is tracked in annual reports and criticized when goals are not met.
